clinicalPearls: PCOS is diagnosed using the Rotterdam criteria, requiring at least two of oligo- or anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound, after excluding mimics
Common presentations include irregular or absent periods, hirsutism and acne, subfertility, and difficulty with weight
Insulin resistance is central to the syndrome and is often present regardless of body weight, though obesity worsens it
It is the leading cause of anovulatory infertility
Unopposed oestrogen from chronic anovulation increases the long-term risk of endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma, so regular endometrial protection is important
Lifestyle modification with weight management is the first-line intervention and can restore ovulation and improve metabolic profile
Management is symptom-directed: cycle regulation and endometrial protection, treatment of hyperandrogenic features, and ovulation induction when fertility is desired
Screening for and managing metabolic complications, including impaired glucose tolerance, type 2 diabetes, and dyslipidaemia, is an essential part of long-term care
reference.pathophysiology: PCOS reflects a complex interplay of hormonal and metabolic disturbances. Insulin resistance with compensatory hyperinsulinaemia stimulates ovarian theca cells to overproduce androgens and reduces hepatic sex hormone-binding globulin, raising free androgen levels. Altered gonadotrophin secretion, with a relatively high luteinising hormone drive, further promotes androgen production and disrupts follicular maturation, so multiple small antral follicles accumulate without a dominant follicle emerging, causing anovulation. Chronic unopposed oestrogen exposure from anovulation places the endometrium at risk of hyperplasia.
additionalInvestigations: Serum total and free testosterone and other androgens
Luteinising hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone, and sex hormone-binding globulin
Thyroid function and prolactin to exclude alternative causes
17-hydroxyprogesterone to screen for non-classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Transvaginal ultrasound for ovarian morphology and antral follicle count
Oral glucose tolerance test and lipid profile to assess metabolic risk
redFlags: Rapid onset or severe virilisation suggesting an androgen-secreting tumour rather than PCOS
Prolonged amenorrhoea with abnormal bleeding raising concern for endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma
Markedly elevated androgens beyond the range typical of PCOS
Severe metabolic derangement such as newly diagnosed diabetes
reference.prognosis: PCOS is a lifelong condition whose reproductive symptoms often improve with weight management and targeted therapy, and many women conceive with or without ovulation induction. The main long-term concerns are metabolic, with increased risks of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and, through chronic anovulation, endometrial cancer; proactive metabolic surveillance improves outcomes.
pitfalls: Diagnosing PCOS without excluding thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia, and other mimics
Relying on ultrasound alone, since polycystic ovarian morphology can occur in healthy women
Overlooking endometrial protection in women with prolonged amenorrhoea
Focusing only on fertility and neglecting long-term metabolic and cardiovascular risk
Attributing severe or rapidly progressive virilisation to PCOS
management: Lifestyle modification with weight management, diet and exercise as first-line, which can restore ovulation and improve the metabolic and androgenic profile
Combined hormonal contraception to regulate cycles, provide endometrial protection and treat hirsutism and acne
Anti-androgen therapy such as spironolactone alongside contraception, with cosmetic measures for hirsutism
Endometrial protection through cyclical progestogen or combined contraception to counter unopposed oestrogen and reduce hyperplasia risk
Ovulation induction for those seeking pregnancy with letrozole first-line or clomifene, and metformin as an adjunct
Metformin and metabolic risk-factor management, with screening for impaired glucose tolerance, diabetes and dyslipidaemia
Long-term cardiovascular risk surveillance and mental health support
Multidisciplinary care across gynaecology, endocrinology and fertility services
